new_statements.quote: Strictly speaking, Eskayan sounds are the idiolectal product of a judgment made by an individual reader. Even so, speakers and reciters of Eskayan exhibit strong consistency in their articulation of Eskayan words. Stress appears to fall on the penultimate syllable, regardless of root length or the presence of prefixes and suffixes (affixation). In Boholano-Visayan, this is also the case, although certain kinds of affixation will shift the stress to the final syllable. [...] There is no contrastive stress in Eskayan, nor is Eskayan /u/ ever realised as [ə]. These so-called 'suprasegmental' phenomena do not, however, play a significant role in either language.
new_statements.citation: Kelly, Piers. 2012. The word made flesh: An ethnographic history of Eskayan, a utopian language and script in the southern Philippines. PhD thesis, The Australian National University, Canberra.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 5 'Sounds and Shapes', section 5.2 'Sounds', pp. 139-140 (PDF pp. 168-169)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is regular on the penultimate syllable of the (affixed) word; unlike its matrix language Boholano-Visayan, affixation does not shift stress to the final syllable and stress is never lexically contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Eskayan; the author hedges ('appears to fall') and notes pronunciation is reading-derived (all speakers are L1 Boholano-Visayan; Eskayan is learned from written texts). Contrast drawn with Visayan, where some affixes shift stress to the final syllable and a few disyllables contrast by stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word including prefixes and suffixes (stress computed over the affixed word, stays penultimate). Based on recitation/reading pronunciation of a non-native auxiliary language; impressionistic, no instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Eskayan (eska1234, ISO esy) as recited/read in the five Eskaya villages of southeast Bohol (Taytay, Biabas, etc.); it is a created auxiliary language whose speakers are all L1 Boholano-Visayan (Cebuano, cebu1242, Bohol dialect), and Kelly explicitly contrasts Eskayan's non-shifting, non-contrastive penultimate stress with Boholano-Visayan.

sources.note: Ch. 5 'Sounds and Shapes', sec. 5.2, pp. 139-140: stress appears to fall on the penultimate syllable regardless of root length or affixation; unlike Boholano-Visayan, affixation does not shift stress and there is no contrastive stress in Eskayan; suprasegmentals 'do not play a significant role'.
Says Eskayan shares all phonemes of Visayan-Boholano and differs in phonotactics (citing Kelly 2006 NCIP report); no stress statement.
